nodes.label: An 81-year-old man presented with cough, fever, shortness of breath, and later developed right-sided ptosis and anisocoria with a miotic right pupil.

An 81-year-old man with medical history of coronary artery disease with coronary artery bypass two years prior, atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.1%).

Initially developed cough, subjective fever, and shortness of breath; was treated with azithromycin for bronchitis, then levofloxacin after a right upper lobe infiltrate was found; symptoms progressed despite antibiotics.

Exposure history: spent time at a Northern Minnesota cabin with minimal outdoor exposure; previous missionary work in Colombia ended two years before admission; never smoked and rarely consumed alcohol.

Physical exam: temperature 38.6°C, pulse 130 beats/min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 114/61 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 82% improving to >90% with 5 L/min oxygen; diminished lung sounds in right upper lobe and diffuse crackles in right lung base; systolic ejection murmur, mild pitting edema to knees bilaterally; no clubbing, cyanosis, cervical/axillary lymphadenopathy; neurologic and skin examinations normal.
Later developed right-sided ptosis and anisocoria with asymmetrically miotic right pupil, more evident in dark environment.
Blastomyces urine antigen test is positive
Histoplasma blood antigen test is positive
Bronchoalveolar lavage GMS stain shows broad-based budding yeast
Chest imaging shows right upper lobe consolidation and left-sided nodules
No cytologic or imaging proof of a mass is found
Pulmonary blastomycosis with disseminated fungal infection
Tuberculosis, cryptococcus, legionella, and influenza-related tests are negative
Head CT/MRI shows no acute intracranial lesions
Right-sided Horner's syndrome is caused by apical inflammatory scarring from pulmonary blastomycosis
Pulmonary blastomycosis with disseminated fungal infection
Radiologist notes Histoplasma blood antigen cross-reacts with Blastomyces, limiting its specificity for histoplasmosis
Species-specific fungal culture, chest CT, and thoracic MRI are pending
